title: The Kahun papyrus on women's health
summary: A papyrus from the town of Lahun in Egypt, written around 1800 BCE, sets out diagnoses and treatments for gynaecological complaints, fertility and pregnancy. It is the oldest surviving Egyptian medical papyrus.
explanation:
The papyrus was excavated at el-Lahun, near the Faiyum, by Flinders Petrie in 1889 and is now in the Petrie Museum at University College London (UC 32057). It dates from the Twelfth Dynasty of the Middle Kingdom.

The text is divided into short sections, each describing a woman's complaint, how to recognise it and how to treat it, with remedies applied to the body or taken by mouth rather than surgery. It also covers fertility, pregnancy and contraception.

Older medical texts exist elsewhere: a Sumerian medical text from around 2000 BCE is known from Mesopotamia.

date.basis: Dated on palaeographic and archaeological grounds to the Twelfth Dynasty (Middle Kingdom), which ended c. 1773 BCE.

whatChanged: Preserves the earliest systematic written guidance on women's reproductive health from Egypt.
whyItMattered: Shows that maternal and reproductive health was a distinct field of medical knowledge nearly four thousand years ago.
limitations: Its explanations reflect Egyptian ideas of the body, such as the womb causing symptoms elsewhere; many remedies would not be effective.
Being the oldest surviving Egyptian medical papyrus says nothing about where such knowledge began.

title: The Edwin Smith papyrus: injuries examined case by case
summary: An Egyptian papyrus copied around 1600 BCE presents 48 cases of wounds and fractures, each with examination, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment. It includes the earliest known written descriptions of the brain's surface and of spinal injury.
explanation:
The scroll is named after the American dealer Edwin Smith, who bought it near Luxor in 1862; it is now held by the New York Academy of Medicine. It was copied around 1600 BCE from an older text whose date is uncertain.

Its 48 cases are ordered from the skull down to the chest and upper arm, and each follows a fixed formula: a description of the injury, the diagnosis, a prognosis and the treatment, with explanatory notes. Several cases describe skull fractures exposing the brain and its coverings, and injuries of the neck that cause paralysis.

The main text is strikingly free of magic, though spells and recipes appear on the other side of the papyrus.

date.basis: The surviving copy is dated to about 1600 BCE. The original it was copied from is older; estimates range widely and are uncertain.

whyItMattered: It is the oldest known surgical treatise and a key witness to Egyptian clinical reasoning.
limitations: It is a copy; the date and authorship of the original are unknown, and the 1862 purchase means its findspot is unrecorded.
Claims that it reflects a 'scientific' medicine separate from magic are partly modern framing; the same scroll contains spells.

title: Babylon's Diagnostic Handbook is edited
summary: Around the mid-eleventh century BCE the Babylonian scholar Esagil-kīn-apli produced a standard edition of Sakikkû, a long series of tablets linking symptoms to diagnoses and prognoses.
explanation:
Mesopotamian healers had been writing down medical knowledge for centuries. Esagil-kīn-apli, chief scholar to King Adad-apla-iddina, gathered and edited the diagnostic omen series known as Sakikkû, 'symptoms', creating the version that later scribes copied. His own catalogue explaining the new edition survives in Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian copies.

Each entry follows a conditional formula: if a patient shows certain signs, then the diagnosis or outcome is this. The handbook covers symptoms throughout the body and records disease names, prognosis and supposed causes, which often included divine or demonic agency alongside natural explanations.

The work shows diagnosis organised as a systematic body of knowledge long before Greek medicine.

date.basis: During the reign of Adad-apla-iddina, as named in Esagil-kīn-apli's catalogue; reign dates themselves vary slightly between chronologies.

locations.name: Babylonia
locations.role: Region where the edition was made; copies survive from Assyria and Babylonia

people.name: Esagil-kīn-apli
people.role: Chief scholar (ummânu) who edited the series

whatChanged: Created a standardised reference that tied observable signs to diagnosis and prognosis.
whyItMattered: One of the earliest large-scale systematisations of diagnosis, and a reminder that diagnostic reasoning did not begin in Greece.
limitations: The handbook mixes clinical observation with divination; its causes are often supernatural.
Esagil-kīn-apli edited an existing tradition rather than composing it from scratch.

title: 'On the Sacred Disease' argues epilepsy is natural
summary: A treatise in the Hippocratic collection, written around 450–400 BCE by an unknown author, insists that epilepsy is no more divine than any other disease and that its seat is the brain.
explanation:
Epilepsy was widely called the 'sacred disease' and treated with purifications and charms. The author of this short treatise attacked that view, arguing that people called the disease divine only because they did not understand it.

He described seizures from observation, loss of voice, foaming at the mouth, clenched hands and loss of awareness, and located their cause in the brain, which he regarded as the organ of thought and feeling. His mechanism, phlegm blocking passages from the brain, came from humoral theory and has not survived, but the insistence on natural causes did.

The treatise belongs to the Hippocratic Corpus, a collection of writings by many authors traditionally linked to Hippocrates of Kos. Its author is not known, and earlier thinkers such as Alcmaeon of Croton had already identified the brain as the seat of intelligence.

date.basis: Usually dated to the second half of the fifth century BCE on stylistic and historical grounds.

locations.name: Greek-speaking Aegean world
locations.role: Author and place of writing unknown; the Corpus is traditionally linked to Kos

whatChanged: Argued explicitly that a feared condition had natural, brain-based causes rather than divine ones.
whyItMattered: An early challenge to supernatural explanations of disease and to the stigma attached to epilepsy, which nonetheless persisted for centuries.
limitations: The proposed mechanism (phlegm from the brain) was wrong.
Attribution to Hippocrates himself is traditional, not established.
Natural and supernatural explanations coexisted in many traditions, including Mesopotamian and Egyptian medicine.

title: Medical manuscripts buried at Mawangdui
summary: A Han-dynasty tomb at Mawangdui, sealed in 168 BCE, held the earliest surviving Chinese medical manuscripts, including a formulary of more than 250 prescriptions now called Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments.
explanation:
Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, near Changsha, probably belonged to Li Xi, a young nobleman of the Western Han. When it was excavated in 1973, a lacquer case in the coffin chamber held a library of texts written on silk, bamboo and wood. Among them were medical manuscripts that had been unknown for two thousand years.

The best known, now called Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments, contains more than 250 prescriptions and treatments. Other manuscripts deal with the body's channels and with treatment by moxa, a plant material burned on or near the skin. Because they predate the classic medical canons, they show Chinese medicine at an earlier, less systematised stage.

The tomb gives a firm latest date; the texts themselves were composed and copied earlier, at dates that are uncertain.

date.basis: The tomb was sealed in 168 BCE, so the manuscripts were written before then. When the texts were composed is uncertain.

locations.name: Mawangdui Tomb 3, near Changsha (Kingdom of Changsha)

whatChanged: Revealed medical writing from before the classic Chinese canons, otherwise lost.
whyItMattered: Changed scholars' understanding of how Chinese medicine developed and when its classic texts were compiled.
limitations: These are the earliest surviving manuscripts, not the beginning of Chinese medical writing.
How well the remedies worked is unknown, and they reflect ideas about illness very different from today's.

title: The Compendium of Suśruta describes surgery, including rebuilding the nose
summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā, a Sanskrit medical treatise composed in layers about two thousand years ago, is a foundation of Ayurveda and contains detailed surgical instructions, including the reconstruction of noses and ears with skin flaps.
explanation:
The Compendium of Suśruta is one of the classical texts of South Asian medicine. It covers diagnosis and therapy but is especially known for its surgical teaching, including the plastic repair of the nose and ears.

Its nasal reconstruction, using a flap of the patient's own skin, was later known in Europe as the 'Indian method'. The text was written in several authorial layers, and later commentators worked with revised versions. The oldest dated manuscript, from 878 CE and preserved in Kathmandu, records an earlier version than modern printed editions.

Popular and clinical literature often dates Suśruta to 600 BCE or even earlier. Philological research does not support these dates.

date.basis: The Suśruta Project dates the work to about two thousand years ago and stresses its many authorial layers; internal evidence suggests it is later than the Carakasaṃhitā. The earliest dated manuscript is from 878 CE. The range shown is deliberately broad.

locations.role: Where the text was composed is not known

people.role: Authors of successive layers of the text

whyItMattered: The Indian method of nasal reconstruction influenced European plastic surgery, and the text remains central to Ayurveda.
limitations: The common clinical claim that Suśruta lived around 600 BCE (or 1000–800 BCE) is not supported by textual scholarship.
The surviving text mixes layers from different periods, so not every technique can be dated to the same time.
contested: Dates for Suśruta and the Compendium vary by more than a millennium across publications; philologists date the work to about two thousand years ago.

title: Tetracycline in the bones of ancient Nubians
summary: Bones from a population that lived in Sudanese Nubia around 350–550 CE contain the antibiotic tetracycline, probably from fermented grain or beer. Whether its use was deliberate is debated.
explanation:
In 1980, examining Nubian bones under ultraviolet light, the anthropologist George Armelagos and colleagues noticed a green-yellow fluorescence typical of tetracycline, an antibiotic produced by Streptomyces soil bacteria. Sceptics argued that the signal could have come from microbes invading the bones after burial.

In 2010, the chemist Mark Nelson and colleagues dissolved samples and confirmed by mass spectrometry that tetracycline was embedded in the bone itself, including in a young child. The quantities suggested regular consumption over long periods. The team proposed that the source was grain fermented into a beer-like gruel and contaminated with Streptomyces.

The authors believe the Nubians knew what they were doing. That is an interpretation: the chemistry shows exposure, not intention or medical purpose.

date.basis: Date range of the burial population studied (the 'X-Group' period).

locationNote: The burial sites lie in Sudanese Nubia; the marker shows the region rather than a specific cemetery.

people.name: Nubian communities of the Nile valley
people.role: Produced and consumed the fermented food or drink

people.name: George Armelagos
people.role: Bioarchaeologist who first noticed the fluorescence

whatChanged: Showed that people ingested an antibiotic substance some 1,500 years before antibiotics were discovered in the laboratory.
whyItMattered: Raises the possibility that fermented foods were used, knowingly or not, in ways that affected infection, and shows how chemistry can test archaeological claims.
limitations: The evidence shows consumption, not that the substance was used as medicine or that it improved health.
The claim that Nubians deliberately produced it is the researchers' interpretation.
contested: Earlier critics attributed the fluorescence to post-burial contamination; the 2010 chemical analysis addressed that, but the question of intent remains open.

title: Two thousand years of skull surgery in the Andes
summary: More trepanned skulls are known from Peru than from the rest of the world combined. Healing on the bone shows survival improved over time, reaching high rates in the centuries before the Spanish conquest.
explanation:
Over 800 skulls with surgical openings have been recovered from burial caves and excavations in coastal and highland Peru, the earliest dating to around 400 BCE. Analysing healing around the openings, John Verano and colleagues showed that early practitioners lost about half their patients, but that techniques were refined over the centuries.

Between about 1000 and 1400 CE, survival rose to as high as 91 per cent in some samples, and in the Inca period only around 17 to 25 per cent of patients died before their skulls began to heal. Some skulls bear several openings.

The researchers note that these outcomes compare favourably with nineteenth-century cranial surgery, but there are no written records explaining how Andean practitioners avoided infection.

whyItMattered: Shows independent development of cranial surgery in the Americas, and that pre-modern surgeons could achieve high survival.
limitations: Healing shows survival, not why the operation was done or whether it helped the patient's condition.
Most skulls were collected in the late 1800s and early 1900s, and their contexts are not always well recorded.

title: Covered drains in every street of Mohenjo-daro
summary: In the third millennium BCE, the Indus city of Mohenjo-daro was built with drains along every street and lane, connected to bathing floors and wastewater chutes in houses.
explanation:
Mohenjo-daro, on the right bank of the Indus, is the best-preserved city of the Indus civilisation. Its lower town was laid out on a strict plan. Street drains of fitted baked brick, sealed with mud mortar, ran along every street and lane, even in the poorest quarters, and were mostly covered with bricks or limestone blocks that could be lifted for cleaning. Larger drains had corbelled roofs high enough for workers to enter.

Inside houses, bathing floors and vertical pipes in the walls carried wastewater out to the street drains. The same drains were maintained and rebuilt over long periods. The so-called Great Bath, a large waterproofed tank, was emptied through a covered drain.

The system shows organised management of water and waste on an urban scale. What its builders understood about the link between waste and disease is unknown.

date.basis: UNESCO dates the city to the 3rd millennium BCE. The drains were built and rebuilt over a long period within this range.

people.name: Inhabitants and builders of the Indus city

whatChanged: Shows city-wide management of wastewater built into urban design.
whyItMattered: One of the earliest known examples of sanitation planned at the scale of a whole city.
limitations: We cannot tell whether health was a motive; the drains may reflect ideas of cleanliness, ritual or simple practicality.
Similar features exist at other Indus cities such as Harappa; Mohenjo-daro is the best preserved, not necessarily the first.

sources.supports: Most ancient and best preserved urban ruin in the Indus Valley, 3rd millennium BC; strictly planned lower town.

title: Ötzi the Iceman carried a medicinal fungus
summary: Ötzi, a man who died in the Alps around 3300 BCE, carried two pieces of birch polypore fungus strung on a leather thong. His gut contained whipworm eggs, and some researchers argue he used the fungus, which has antibacterial and anti-parasite properties, as medicine.
explanation:
Ötzi's body was found in 1991 in a glacier on the border between Austria and Italy, preserved with his clothing and equipment. Examination showed that he had been infected with whipworm, an intestinal parasite, as well as other ailments.

Among his belongings were two fragments of the birch polypore (Fomitopsis betulina), pierced and threaded on a strip of leather. In 1998 the palaeopathologist Luigi Capasso suggested in The Lancet that Ötzi used it as a natural laxative and antibiotic, perhaps against the worms. The fungus has a long history in European folk medicine, and laboratory studies have found antibacterial and anti-inflammatory compounds in it.

whyItMattered: Ötzi's equipment is among the oldest direct evidence that people may have carried medicines with them.
limitations: There is no direct evidence of how Ötzi used the fungus; other purposes are possible.
Fungi with medicinal properties may have been used much earlier, but such evidence rarely survives.
contested: Whether the fungus was medicine is debated: some researchers see a 'medicine kit', while others doubt that it was used for treatment at all.

title: Specialist physicians at the Egyptian royal court
summary: Inscriptions from Egypt's Old Kingdom give physicians specialised titles. Iry, a Sixth Dynasty court doctor (c. 2300 BCE), was physician of the eyes and of the belly and 'shepherd of the king's rectum'. Two thousand years later Herodotus wrote that every Egyptian physician treated a single disease.
explanation:
Egyptian physicians (swnw) held ranked titles, and some were associated with particular parts of the body. Iry's inscriptions describe him as senior physician of the palace, physician of the eyes and of the belly, and guardian of the royal rectum, a role that included giving enemas to the king.

A study of known Egyptian physicians found that 12 of 42 from the Old Kingdom held titles indicating a speciality, and some claimed several. When Herodotus visited Egypt in the fifth century BCE he reported that medicine was divided so that each physician treated one disorder only, although historians treat this claim with caution.

whatChanged: Medical work was divided among practitioners with recognised areas of expertise.
whyItMattered: Egypt offers some of the earliest evidence of an organised medical profession with specialists.
limitations: Titles may describe court roles rather than specialist training in the modern sense.
Herodotus visited about two thousand years later, and his claim that each doctor treated only one disease is exaggerated: many physicians held several titles.

title: The Nineveh Medical Encyclopaedia in Ashurbanipal's library
summary: In the seventh century BCE scholars of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembled at Nineveh a structured medical handbook of about fifty tablets, arranged in treatises from head to foot, with thousands of symptoms and prescriptions drawn from older Babylonian tradition.
explanation:
Mesopotamian medicine had been written down for more than a thousand years, and Ashurbanipal, who reigned from 669 to about 630 BCE, set out to collect all scholarly knowledge in his library. His scholars edited existing medical texts into new standard editions and arranged them, according to a surviving ancient catalogue, into a series of twelve treatises.

The tablets were broken when Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE and lay buried until excavated in the nineteenth century; many are now in the British Museum. Only recently have researchers reconstructed the whole encyclopaedia from its fragments.

date.basis: Compiled during the reign of Ashurbanipal.

whatChanged: Medical knowledge was gathered into a single systematic, organised reference work.
whyItMattered: It is described as the most standardised and systematic body of medical writing known before Galen.
limitations: It drew on earlier Babylonian texts; much of its content is older than the library.
Remedies were combined with incantations and ritual.

sources.supports: A 2,600-year-old handbook with thousands of descriptions of diseases and symptoms and prescriptions; compiled in the library of Ashurbanipal; made up of 12 sections.

title: Hammurabi's laws set surgeons' fees and penalties
summary: The law code of Hammurabi, king of Babylon around 1755 BCE, fixed what a physician could charge for a successful operation with a bronze lancet, according to the patient's status, and decreed that a surgeon whose operation killed a free man should lose his hand.
explanation:
Among the code's 282 laws, a group from §215 deals with healers. A physician who saved a free man's life by a major operation, or saved his eye by opening it with a bronze lancet, received ten shekels of silver; less was paid for a commoner or a slave. Setting a broken bone earned five shekels from a free man.

If the operation killed a free man or destroyed his eye, the physician's hand was to be cut off; if a slave died, he had to replace the slave.

date.basis: Hammurabi reigned c. 1792–1750 BCE; the code dates from late in his reign.

whatChanged: Medical treatment was regulated by law, with fixed fees and penalties for harm.
whyItMattered: It is among the earliest known legal rules on medical fees and liability for harm to patients.
limitations: The laws show how surgery was regulated, not how often operations were done or how they were performed.
Penalties and fees depended on social class, so patients were not treated equally.

sources.citation: NinMed (ORACC, University of Pennsylvania). Surgery: information from texts, quoting Roth 1995.

title: The Ebers Papyrus and Egypt's other medical papyri
summary: The Ebers Papyrus, a 20-metre scroll written in Egypt around 1550 BCE, is the most extensive surviving record of ancient Egyptian medicine. It gathers some 700 remedies and spells and a treatise on the heart and its vessels. Other papyri, such as the Hearst, London and Berlin papyri, preserve related texts.
explanation:
The scroll's 110 pages hold some 700 magical formulas and folk remedies, for complaints ranging from crocodile bites to toenail pain, as well as a treatise on the heart and its vessels and a chapter on disorders such as depression. A calendar on the back mentions the ninth year of King Amenhotep I. It was reportedly found in a tomb in the Assasif area of the Theban necropolis and was bought by the Egyptologist Georg Ebers, who published it in 1875.

Later medical papyri overlap with it: the Hearst Papyrus from the reign of Thutmose III; the London Medical Papyrus, dated to Tutankhamun's reign; and the Berlin or Brugsch Papyrus of about 1300 BCE.

date.basis: Dated by a calendar referring to year 9 of Amenhotep I; the other papyri date from c. 1450 to 1300 BCE.

people.name: Georg Ebers
people.role: Egyptologist who bought and published the papyrus

people.name: Edwin Smith
people.role: American dealer in Luxor who owned it first

whatChanged: It preserves the fullest picture of how Egyptian doctors understood and treated disease.
whyItMattered: The Egyptian medical papyri are among the oldest medical books to survive, giving a detailed picture of a medical tradition that combined practical remedies with magic.
limitations: It is believed to be copied from earlier texts, so its contents are older than the scroll.
Its circumstances of discovery rest on a dealer's account and are uncertain.

title: Saffron frescoes at Akrotiri on Thera
summary: Wall paintings in the building called Xeste 3 at Akrotiri, a Bronze Age town on Thera (Santorini) buried by a volcanic eruption around 1600 BCE, show women gathering saffron crocus flowers and offering them to a goddess. Some scholars interpret them as the earliest images of a medicinal plant being prepared.
explanation:
The frescoes show girls and women picking crocuses in a rocky landscape and bringing them in baskets to a seated goddess, flanked by a griffin and a monkey. Xeste 3 was a large, richly decorated building, probably used for rituals.

In 2004 the art historian Susan Ferrence and the cardiologist Gordon Bendersky argued that the scenes depict the stages of producing saffron as a drug and show a goddess of healing. Saffron was later used in medicine, appearing in the Ebers Papyrus and in Dioscorides' first-century herbal.

date.basis: The town flourished around 1600 BCE before it was buried by the eruption of Thera.

people.name: Susan Ferrence and Gordon Bendersky
people.role: Researchers who proposed the medicinal interpretation

whatChanged: If the interpretation is right, the frescoes show a plant being gathered and processed for its healing value.
whyItMattered: They are cited as possible early visual evidence for the medicinal use of plants in the Mediterranean.
limitations: Earlier studies of the frescoes relied mainly on the images themselves, which can support several readings.
Saffron was also valued as a dye, food and ritual offering.
contested: Whether the frescoes show medicine is disputed: they have also been read as scenes of ritual and fertility, or of perfume and spice production.

sources.citation: Day J. Crocuses in context: a diachronic survey of the crocus motif in the Aegean Bronze Age. Hesperia 80(3):337 (2011).

title: Udjahorresnet restores the medical 'House of Life' at Sais
summary: Around 519 BCE the Persian king Darius I sent the Egyptian chief physician Udjahorresnet back to Egypt to restore the 'House of Life' at Sais, a temple institution where physicians were trained and texts kept. His inscribed statue, now in the Vatican, records the commission.
explanation:
Udjahorresnet, whose titles included chief physician, treasurer and commander of the king's fleet, served the Persian kings who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE. According to the inscription on his naophorous statue (a figure holding a small shrine), Darius ordered him to return home and restore the houses of life that had fallen into ruin.

One recent study links the order to Darius's dissatisfaction with Egyptian physicians, who, according to Herodotus, had failed to cure his injured ankle.

date.basis: Darius I came to the throne in 522 BCE; the statue was probably made soon after Udjahorresnet's return.

people.name: Udjahorresnet
people.role: Chief physician and priest of Neith

whatChanged: A royal order restored an institution for training physicians and keeping medical texts.
whyItMattered: It is one of the clearest records of an ancient state supporting medical education.
limitations: The nature of the House of Life is debated; it was a temple scriptorium and school, not a medical school in the modern sense.
The statue's provenance is assumed rather than known.

sources.citation: Livius.org. Wedjahor-Resne (Udjahorresnet) and his inscription.
sources.supports: Naophoros statue about 70 cm high, brought to Italy by Hadrian, now in the Vatican Museums; Darius allowed him to return and ordered him to supervise the destroyed 'houses of life'; statue probably made soon after his return.

sources.citation: Vatican Museums. The 'Vatican Naophorous'.
sources.supports: Statue of Udjahorresnet, chief physician and commander of the king's fleet, holding a naos; provenance unknown but assumed to be Sais.

title: Medicinal tablets survive in a Roman-era shipwreck
summary: A ship that sank off Populonia in Tuscany around 140 BCE carried a physician's supplies, including a tin box of flat grey tablets. Chemical analysis published in 2013 showed they were mainly zinc compounds mixed with starch, fats and pine resin, probably an eye medicine.
explanation:
The Pozzino wreck, found in 1974 in the Gulf of Baratti and excavated in 1989–90, held a small mortar, a bronze cupping vessel, an iron probe, 136 wooden vials and many tin boxes, evidently a medical kit.

Researchers analysed the discoid tablets, each about 4 cm across, and found that the zinc minerals hydrozincite and smithsonite made up most of their mineral content. Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides describe zinc compounds being used for the eyes and skin, and the tablets' shape matches the Latin collyrium, from a Greek word for small round loaves, used for eye remedies.

date.basis: The wreck is dated to the second century BCE, about 140 BCE.

whatChanged: It provides physical evidence of a manufactured medicine in measured, portable doses.
whyItMattered: Ancient medicines rarely survive; these tablets let researchers compare ancient recipes with an actual preparation.
limitations: Written recipes for pills and tablets are known from earlier sources; this is a rare surviving example, not the first use.
How the tablets were used is inferred from their composition and from ancient texts.

sources.citation: Giachi G, Pallecchi P, Romualdi A, et al. Ingredients of a 2,000-y-old medicine revealed by chemical, mineralogical, and botanical investigations. PNAS 110(4):1193–1196 (2013).
sources.supports: Tin pyxis from the Pozzino shipwreck (second century BC) with six flat grey discoid tablets; hydrozincite and smithsonite the most abundant ingredients, with starch, lipids and pine resin; probably ophthalmic, the collyrium.

sources.citation: Mariotti Lippi M, Giachi G. Pollen content in a II century BC remedy from the Pozzino shipwreck. Palynology 45(1) (2021).
sources.supports: Wreck in the Gulf of Baratti near Piombino at about 18 m, near Etruscan Populonia; mortar, bronze cupping vessel, iron probe, tin pyxides and 136 wooden vials.

title: Alcmaeon of Croton places understanding in the brain
summary: Around 500 BCE Alcmaeon of Croton, in a Greek city in southern Italy famed for its physicians, argued that the brain is the seat of understanding and that the senses are linked to it by channels. Ancient writers say he cut out an animal's eye and saw such a channel, probably the optic nerve.
explanation:
Croton's physicians were reputed in the sixth century BCE to be the best in the Greek world. Alcmaeon, who wrote mainly on medical matters, held that sense organs were connected to the brain by passages (poroi), and distinguished human understanding from the perception that animals also share. Later sources report that he excised an animal's eye to examine its nature.

Plato and later the Hippocratic writers accepted that the brain was the organ of thought, though Aristotle placed it in the heart.

date.basis: Alcmaeon was active in the late sixth or early fifth century BCE.

whatChanged: The brain, rather than the heart, was proposed as the organ of perception and thought.
whyItMattered: The view that the brain governs sensation and understanding was taken up by the Hippocratic writers and Alexandrian anatomists and is the basis of neuroscience.
limitations: His work survives only in fragments quoted by later authors.
It is doubtful that he used dissection systematically; claims that he was the first to dissect rest on late reports.

sources.citation: Huffman C. Alcmaeon. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
sources.supports: The first to identify the brain as the seat of understanding and to distinguish understanding from perception; doubt that he used dissection as a standard method; Herodotus on Croton's physicians; wrote mostly on medical matters.

sources.citation: Huffman C. Alcmaeon (spring 2007 archive). Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
sources.supports: Sensory organs connected to the brain by channels; may have discovered the optic nerve by excising an animal's eyeball.

sources.citation: Alcmaeon of Croton (c. 540–500 BCE). Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Encyclopedia.com).
sources.supports: May have excised an eyeball and observed passages leading towards the brain; first in the Greek tradition to argue that the brain was the seat of thought; no evidence of systematic dissection.

sources.citation: Gross CG. Aristotle on the brain. The Neuroscientist 1:245–250 (1995).
sources.supports: Aristotle placed sensation in the heart, unlike his predecessors such as Alcmaeon; Alcmaeon described the optic nerves.

sources.supports: Croton known for an early school of medicine; cut out the eye of an animal; inferred channels connecting the eye to the brain.

title: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon (Huangdi Neijing)
summary: The Huangdi Neijing, compiled in Han-dynasty China probably in the first century BCE from older material, set out the theory of Chinese medicine: yin and yang, the five phases, the circulation of qi through channels, diagnosis and acupuncture. It remains the foundational classic of Chinese medicine.
explanation:
The work is written as dialogues between the legendary Yellow Emperor and his ministers. It consists of two books: the Suwen ('Plain Questions'), on medical theory and diagnosis, and the Lingshu ('Divine Pivot'), mainly on acupuncture. Each has 81 chapters.

Tradition dates it to remote antiquity, and Chinese scholars trace its first versions to the Warring States period, with additions under the Qin and Han. Historians now generally regard it as a compilation of shorter texts from different medical lineages made under the Han. Manuscripts buried at Mawangdui in 168 BCE show an earlier stage of the ideas it systematised.

date.basis: Most historians date the compilation to the Han dynasty, probably the first century BCE; earlier layers may date from the Warring States period.

locationNote: The place of compilation is unknown; mapped broadly to the Han heartland around Chang'an.
whatChanged: Chinese medical ideas were gathered into a canon that defined theory, diagnosis and treatment for later physicians.
whyItMattered: It has been the doctrinal foundation of Chinese and East Asian medicine for two thousand years.
limitations: It has no single author or date; the texts were revised and re-edited over centuries.
Earlier medical manuscripts, such as those from Mawangdui, show that many of its ideas developed before it was compiled.

sources.citation: UNESCO Memory of the World Register. Huang Di Nei Jing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon), nomination 2010-15.
sources.supports: The earliest and most important written work of traditional Chinese medicine; two parts, Suwen and Lingshu, each with 9 volumes and 81 chapters; editions in the Warring States period with supplements under the Qin and Han.

sources.citation: Medicine in early China (chapter). Cambridge University Press (Cambridge Core).
sources.supports: The primary canon of East Asian medicine; traced by tradition to a prehistoric sage; Suwen focuses on cosmological theory and Lingshu on acupuncture; Western Han consolidation of knowledge and attribution to legendary sages; most ancient medical works have no definite author.

sources.citation: Traditional Chinese medicine overview citing Sivin (1998). Rukasu Budo Dojo, healing arts.
sources.supports: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon, the oldest received work of Chinese medical theory, was compiled around the first century BCE from shorter texts from different medical lineages.

title: Praxagoras distinguishes arteries from veins
summary: Praxagoras of Cos, a physician active around 340 BCE, distinguished arteries from veins and drew attention to the pulse as a guide to diagnosis. He wrongly thought arteries carried air (pneuma) rather than blood, but his pupil Herophilus built on his work in Alexandria.
explanation:
Born into a medical family on Cos, Praxagoras held that the veins arose from the liver and carried blood made from digested food, while the arteries arose from the heart and carried pneuma, the breath of life. He believed the arteries pulsed by themselves, independently of the heart, and studied the pulse in health and disease.

His pupil Herophilus showed that the walls of arteries are thicker than those of veins, held that arteries contain blood, and transferred to the nerves the role in movement that Praxagoras had given the arteries. Galen later demonstrated that arteries carry blood.

date.basis: Praxagoras flourished around 340 BCE.

whatChanged: The two kinds of blood vessel were recognised as different, and the pulse became a diagnostic sign.
whyItMattered: Pulse diagnosis became central to Greek and later medicine, and the arterial–venous distinction framed anatomy until Harvey.
limitations: His belief that arteries carried air was wrong, as Galen later showed.
His works survive only in fragments quoted by later authors.
Diocles of Carystus is also credited with the distinction, so priority is shared.

sources.citation: Praxagoras of Cos. Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (Encyclopedia.com).
sources.supports: Born on Cos c. 340 BC into a medical family; blood in the veins, psychic pneuma in the arteries from the heart; generally credited with the distinction between veins and arteries; shared views with Diocles; influence on Herophilus.

sources.citation: University at Buffalo, History of CDS. Praxagoras c. 340–280 BC.
sources.supports: Distinguished arteries and veins; arteries carry pneuma and stem from the heart, veins carry blood and stem from the liver; first to direct attention to the pulse in diagnosis; believed arteries pulsed by themselves; refuted by Herophilus.

sources.citation: Porter R. The Greatest Benefit to Mankind (HarperCollins, 1997).
sources.supports: Herophilus a student of Praxagoras (fl. 340 BC), who distinguished arteries from veins; arteries as air tubes; Herophilus noted thicker arterial walls and held that arteries contained blood.

sources.citation: Herophilus. Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (Encyclopedia.com).
sources.supports: Herophilus studied under Praxagoras; Praxagoras and Diocles distinguished arteries and veins; Herophilus transferred to the nerves the function Praxagoras assigned to the arteries.

title: Critobulus removes an arrow from Philip II's eye
summary: During the siege of Methone around 354 BCE, King Philip II of Macedon was struck in the right eye by an arrow. His surgeon, Critobulus of Cos, extracted it so skilfully that, although the eye was lost, Philip's face was not disfigured, according to Pliny the Elder.
explanation:
Philip, father of Alexander the Great, was hit while inspecting siege engines at Methone, a city on the Thermaic Gulf. Pliny, writing four centuries later, praised Critobulus for removing the arrow without leaving a deformity, a celebrated example of ancient battlefield surgery.

A modern study of the evidence discusses how the wound to the cheekbone and eye socket was treated. The case illustrates the skill of Greek surgeons in treating weapon wounds.

date.basis: The siege of Methone lasted from late 355 to early 354 BCE.

whatChanged: It is a documented example of skilled surgical treatment of a penetrating wound to the face.
whyItMattered: It shows the standing of trained surgeons at royal courts and in war in the fourth century BCE.
limitations: The only account of the operation comes from Pliny, written about 400 years later.
Details such as the arrow's inscription come from later anecdote.

sources.citation: Pliny the Elder. Natural History 7.37 (Bostock and Riley translation).
sources.supports: Critobulus extracted an arrow from the eye of King Philip with so much skill that, although the sight was lost, there was no defect.

sources.citation: Smith W (ed.). A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1890): Critobulus.
sources.supports: A Greek surgeon who, according to Pliny, extracted an arrow from Philip's eye, probably at the siege of Methone, preventing disfigurement.

sources.citation: The facial injury of King Philip II of Macedonia and its treatment by Critobulos. Craniomaxillofacial Trauma & Reconstruction 10(3) (2017), MDPI.
sources.supports: Evidence on Philip II's facial injury and its treatment by his physician Critobulos; zygomatico-orbital injury and loss of the eye at Methone; Demosthenes' account of the archer.

sources.citation: HistoryOfWar.org. Siege of Methone, late 355 – early 354 BC.
sources.supports: Methone on the Thermaic Gulf; Philip lost his right eye to an arrow during the siege.

title: Herophilus and Erasistratus dissect human bodies in Alexandria
summary: In early third-century BCE Alexandria, under Ptolemaic patronage, Herophilus and Erasistratus systematically dissected human bodies. They described the nerves and traced them to the brain, distinguished its parts, and studied the eye and heart. Later writers accused them of vivisecting condemned criminals.
explanation:
Greek physicians had dissected animals, but taboos prevented human dissection. In Alexandria, newly founded and home to a great library, the first Ptolemaic kings allowed physicians to dissect the bodies of condemned criminals for some decades. Herophilus of Chalcedon, a pupil of Praxagoras, reportedly carried out hundreds of dissections; he distinguished nerves from blood vessels and tendons, concluded that the brain controlled the body, described the eye and the reproductive organs, and noted the thicker walls of arteries.

Erasistratus of Ceos distinguished sensory from motor nerves, traced both to the brain, and is often called the first experimental physiologist. After their time human dissection was abandoned for some 1,800 years, until the Renaissance.

date.basis: Herophilus (c. 330–260 BCE) and Erasistratus (c. 304–250 BCE) worked under Ptolemy I and Ptolemy II.

whatChanged: Human anatomy was studied directly from human bodies rather than inferred from animals.
whyItMattered: Their discoveries about the nervous system, brain and eye were the most accurate anatomy of antiquity and were passed on through Galen.
limitations: Their writings are lost and known only through later authors such as Galen and Celsus.
Alcmaeon may have dissected earlier, but Herophilus is regarded as the first to dissect human bodies systematically.
contested: Celsus, writing some 250 years later, and Tertullian claimed that they cut open living criminals; some historians accept this, while others regard it as speculation.
harms: If the ancient reports are true, condemned prisoners were dissected alive.

sources.citation: Bay NSY, Bay BH. Greek anatomist Herophilus: the father of anatomy. Anatomy & Cell Biology (2010).
sources.supports: First person to perform systematic dissection of the human body; human dissection permitted for 30 to 40 years before being abandoned for 1,800 years; differentiated nerves from blood vessels and tendons; Celsus and Galen's charges; pupil of Praxagoras.

sources.citation: Wills A. Herophilus, Erasistratus, and the birth of neuroscience (The neuroanatomy of Herophilus). European Neurology 69(5):292 (Karger).
sources.supports: Herophilus (c. 330–260 BC), the 'Father of Anatomy'; cadaveric dissection and possibly vivisection; for 40 years Ptolemaic royal patronage permitted dissection of condemned criminals; library of some 7,000 scrolls.

sources.citation: Bibliotheca Alexandrina, SCIplanet. Herophilus and Erasistratus: the butchers of Alexandria.
sources.supports: Systematic human dissection in third-century BCE Alexandria; nerves traced to the brain as the controlling organ; Erasistratus born on Cos in 304 BCE; Celsus's account of vivisection written 250 years later.

sources.citation: Štrkalj G, Chorn D. Herophilus of Chalcedon and the practice of dissection in Hellenistic Alexandria. South African Medical Journal 98(2) (2008), excerpted.
sources.supports: Herophilus and Erasistratus performed human dissections; no fewer than 600 dissections reported; Celsus claims vivisection.

sources.citation: The first medical encyclopaedia and the experimental physiology of Erasistratus. Project MUSE.
sources.supports: Herophilus and Erasistratus probably the first to demonstrate human dissection; Celsus's account; Erasistratus distinguished sensory from motor nerves and traced both to the brain; considered the first experimental physiologist.

sources.citation: Herophilos of Chalcedon (review). DergiPark.
sources.supports: Celsus and Tertullian blamed Herophilos for vivisection on condemned criminals, but such accusations remain speculative.

title: Huangfu Mi's systematic classic of acupuncture
summary: In the third century CE the scholar Huangfu Mi compiled the Zhenjiu Jiayi Jing (A–B Classic of Acupuncture and Moxibustion), reorganising earlier texts into the first systematic, surviving book devoted to acupuncture and moxibustion, with standardised names and locations of points.
explanation:
Huangfu Mi (215–282), born in what is now Gansu province, turned to medicine after acupuncture helped his own illness. He compared three earlier works, the Huangdi Zhenjing, the Suwen and a lost Mingtang text on acupuncture points, and arranged their material by topic.

Earlier acupuncture writings disagreed about the names and positions of points. His 12-volume compilation, probably assembled between 256 and 282, classified the points systematically and became the basis for later acupuncture teaching in China and East Asia.

date.basis: Sources date the compilation to 256–260 or to about 282.

locationNote: Mapped to Huangfu Mi's birthplace; where he compiled the work is not recorded in the sources consulted.
whatChanged: Acupuncture points and techniques were organised into a coherent reference work.
whyItMattered: It became a standard text for acupuncture and preserved material from earlier works that are now lost.
limitations: It compiled earlier texts rather than adding new methods.
Acupuncture had developed earlier, from at least the second or first century BCE.

sources.citation: Does modern research concerning Chinese medicine acupoints relate to original prescriptions? (abstract). J Altern Complement Med (2019), via Read by QxMD.
sources.supports: Huang Fu Mi's Zhen Jiu Jia Yi Jing regarded as the earliest text (282 CE) on differential diagnosis and clinical acumoxa therapy.

sources.citation: Bi W. Huangfu Mi: ancestor of acupuncture. Science and Technology Daily (2022).
sources.supports: Huangfu Mi (215–282); earliest acupuncture books had errors in names and locations of points; compiled the Systematic Classic in 256–260, the earliest systemised book on acupuncture and moxibustion, in 12 volumes.

sources.citation: China Culture. Huangfu Mi.
sources.supports: Born in 215 in Anding Chaona (now Lingtai, Gansu); acupuncture treated his own illness; compared the Huangdi Zhenjing, Su Wen and the Mingtang acupuncture text.

title: Zhang Zhongjing's Treatise on Cold Damage
summary: Around 200 CE, amid war and epidemics at the end of the Han dynasty, the physician Zhang Zhongjing wrote the Shanghan Zabing Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Disorders). It linked patterns of symptoms to specific herbal prescriptions and became the foundation of clinical practice in Chinese medicine.
explanation:
Zhang (c. 150–219), from Nanyang in present-day Henan, wrote after epidemics killed many of his own family. Drawing on the Huangdi Neijing, prescriptions he had collected and his own experience, he classified febrile illnesses by stages and patterns and matched each to a treatment.

The original was lost in the wars of the Three Kingdoms period. Later physicians reassembled it as two books, the Shanghan Lun on febrile disease and the Jingui Yaolüe on other disorders, and more than a thousand scholars have since edited and commented on it.

date.basis: Written late in Zhang's life, around 200 CE.

whatChanged: Treatment was tied to systematic recognition of patterns of illness, with fixed prescriptions for each.
whyItMattered: Its formulas and method of pattern-based diagnosis remain central to Chinese herbal medicine.
limitations: Very little is reliably known about Zhang's life.
The text survives only in later reconstructions, so its original form is uncertain.

sources.citation: Bi W. Zhang Zhongjing: the sage of Chinese medicine. Science and Technology Daily (2022).
sources.supports: Zhang (150–219) born in Nanyang, Henan, in the late Eastern Han; used the Huangdi Neijing, collected prescriptions and drew on experience to write the Shanghan Zabing Lun; principle of pattern-based treatment.

title: The Charaka Samhita, a foundation of Ayurvedic medicine
summary: The Charaka Samhita, a Sanskrit compendium of internal medicine probably compiled between about 100 BCE and 200 CE and completed later by Dridhabala, set out Ayurvedic theory, diagnosis, diet, drugs and the ethics of physicians. With the Sushruta Samhita it is one of the two foundational texts of Ayurveda.
explanation:
Tradition holds that the teachings of the sage Atreya were written down by his pupil Agnivesha, and that Charaka revised and expanded that lost work. Centuries later Dridhabala, from Panchanadapura, completed and partly rewrote it, so the text has several layers from different periods.

It contains more than 8,400 verses and concentrates on internal medicine (kayachikitsa), explaining health and disease through the balance of bodily humours and digestion. It covers the causes and signs of disease, prognosis, preventive regimen, hundreds of medicinal substances and the training and conduct of physicians.

date.basis: Meulenbeld's dating of Charaka's recension; Dridhabala's completion is later, perhaps fourth to sixth century CE.

locationNote: Where the text was compiled is not known; mapped broadly to northern South Asia.

people.name: Dridhabala
people.role: Later reviser who completed the text

whatChanged: Indian medical knowledge was organised into a systematic compendium covering theory, diagnosis, treatment and ethics.
whyItMattered: It remains a core text of Ayurveda, still studied by practitioners in India and beyond.
limitations: Its dates are uncertain, and it combines layers written centuries apart.
Ayurvedic theories of humours are not supported by modern biology, though some remedies have been studied scientifically.

sources.supports: Meulenbeld dates the Charaka recension to roughly 100 BCE–200 CE, working over the older Agnivesha Samhita of the Atreya school; final completion by Dridhabala c. 4th–6th century CE; a layered work.

title: Varro suggests that invisible creatures cause disease
summary: In his book on farming, written around 37 BCE, the Roman scholar Marcus Terentius Varro warned against building near swamps, where 'minute creatures' too small to see float in the air, enter the body through the mouth and nose, and cause serious diseases.
explanation:
Varro, one of the most learned men of the Roman Republic and head of Rome's public library, wrote De re rustica as a practical guide to running a country estate. In discussing where to site a farmhouse, he explained the long-observed danger of marshes by invisible living things carried in the air.

The idea echoed Greek atomist speculation about invisible particles. It had little influence at the time, but it resembles the contagion theory later proposed by Girolamo Fracastoro in 1546 and, much later, germ theory. Marshes were in fact dangerous because they bred the mosquitoes that carry malaria.

date.basis: De re rustica was written around 37–36 BCE.

whatChanged: Disease was attributed to invisible living things entering the body from the environment.
whyItMattered: It is one of the earliest clear statements of the idea that tiny organisms cause disease.
limitations: Varro had no way to observe such creatures; the idea was speculation.
Earlier writers, including Greek atomists and, more vaguely, the Indian Atharvaveda, had speculated about invisible causes.

sources.citation: Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh. The history of germ theory in the College collections.
sources.supports: Varro (116–27 BC), director of the library at Rome and author of a work on agriculture, warned against homesteads near swamps because of minute creatures invisible to the eye that float in the air and enter the body through the mouth and nose; Fracastoro's later seminaria.

sources.supports: The idea that diseases are caused by minute living creatures goes back more than 2,000 years; Varro's statement.

title: Celsus's De Medicina, a Roman encyclopedia of medicine
summary: In the early first century CE the Roman writer Aulus Cornelius Celsus wrote De Medicina, an eight-book survey of diet, drugs and surgery that preserves much of Hellenistic medicine. It describes the four signs of inflammation. Lost for centuries, it was rediscovered in 1426–27 and printed in Florence in 1478.
explanation:
De Medicina was one part of a larger encyclopedia, the rest of which is mostly lost. It begins with a history of medicine and a discussion of medical method, including the debate over dissection and vivisection in Alexandria, then covers general pathology, specific diseases, pharmacology and surgery, from removing weapons and stones to amputation. It names the cardinal signs of inflammation: redness, heat, swelling and pain.

It was little known in the later Middle Ages. Manuscripts surfaced in Siena in 1426 and Milan in 1427, and it was among the first medical books to be printed, which gave it great influence in the Renaissance.

date.basis: Celsus wrote under the emperors Augustus or Tiberius; the text was rediscovered in 1426–27 and printed in 1478.

whatChanged: Greek medical knowledge was presented systematically in Latin for Roman readers.
whyItMattered: It is the best surviving account of Hellenistic medicine and surgery, and its printing in 1478 made it a key Renaissance text.
limitations: It is doubtful whether Celsus practised medicine himself.
It was little read for much of the Middle Ages, so its influence came mainly after its rediscovery.
It is sometimes called the first medical book to be printed; it was one of the first, in the 1470s.

sources.citation: HistoryofInformation.com. Celsus's De Medicina, the oldest Western medical document after the Hippocratic writings, and how it survived the Middle Ages.
sources.supports: Lost during the Middle Ages and rediscovered in 1426–27; manuscript at Siena in 1426 and Codex F in 1427; first printed in Florence by Nicolaus Laurentii in 1478.

sources.supports: Oldest copies from the 9th century; first printed in the late 1400s in Florence; after the Hippocratic writings, the oldest surviving medical text.

title: Dioscorides' De Materia Medica
summary: Between about 50 and 70 CE Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek physician from Anazarbus who served with the Roman army, wrote De Materia Medica, describing some 600 plants and other substances and their medicinal uses. It remained the leading reference on drugs for about 1,500 years.
explanation:
Travelling widely with the army, Dioscorides observed many plants and their effects. His five books describe each substance's appearance, habitat, preparation and uses, covering plants, oils and minerals.

The work was copied and used throughout the Middle Ages, often with illustrations; the oldest surviving copy, the Vienna Dioscurides, was made in Constantinople around 512 CE. Renaissance scholars such as Pietro Andrea Mattioli wrote extensive commentaries on it, and it shaped European pharmacy into the early modern period.

date.basis: Usually dated to the reign of Nero or shortly after.

locationNote: Mapped to Dioscorides' birthplace; he gathered material while travelling with the Roman army.
whatChanged: Knowledge of medicinal substances was gathered into a detailed, practical reference.
whyItMattered: It was the most authoritative text on drugs in Europe and the Middle East until the early modern period.
limitations: Many of his plant descriptions are hard to match to modern species.
It reflects traditional knowledge, not tested evidence of effectiveness.

sources.citation: University of Virginia, Claude Moore Health Sciences Library. Pedanius Dioscorides of Anazarbos (fl. 50–70).
sources.supports: A Greek surgeon who served in Nero's army; an extensive guide to pharmacy and medical botany; the classic text for 1,500 years; more than 600 plants and plant ingredients.

sources.citation: Semmelweis Museum. Pictures from the Past of the Healing Arts: guide to the exhibition. Orvostörténeti Közlemények Suppl. 18–19 (2000).

title: Galen builds medicine on anatomy and experiment
summary: Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE), physician to gladiators and later to Roman emperors, combined Hippocratic medicine with anatomy and experiment. Dissecting and experimenting on animals, he showed that arteries carry blood and that the brain controls the voice. His writings dominated medicine for some 1,400 years.
explanation:
After studying in Pergamon and Alexandria, Galen returned to Pergamon in 157 to treat the gladiators of the high priest of Asia, which taught him much about wounds. In 162 he moved to Rome, where he served Marcus Aurelius and later emperors.

Because human dissection was not allowed, he dissected apes, pigs and other animals. In public demonstrations he cut the recurrent laryngeal nerve of a squealing pig to show that the brain controls the voice, cut the spinal cord at different levels to show its role, and showed that arteries contain blood, not air. His theory of the humours and his physiology, some of it wrong, became the basis of medical teaching in the Byzantine, Islamic and European worlds until Vesalius and Harvey.

date.basis: From his appointment as gladiators' physician in 157 to his late career in Rome.

whatChanged: Anatomy and experiment became central to medical argument, and several key physiological facts were demonstrated.
whyItMattered: Galen's writings were the authority for medical theory and practice in Europe and the Middle East from late antiquity to the seventeenth century.
limitations: Because he dissected animals, some of his human anatomy was wrong, as Vesalius later showed.
Some blood in the arteries had been suspected earlier; Galen was the one to demonstrate it.

sources.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica. Galen.
sources.supports: Dominant influence on medicine from the Middle Ages to the mid-17th century; returned to Pergamum in 157 as chief physician to the gladiators of the high priest of Asia; moved to Rome in 162; served Marcus Aurelius, Commodus and Septimius Severus; tied off the recurrent laryngeal nerve; spinal cord transections.

title: Oribasius compiles the Medical Collections
summary: Oribasius (c. 320–c. 403), physician to the emperor Julian, compiled at Julian's request a 70-book Greek medical encyclopedia of excerpts from earlier writers. Only part of it survives, but it preserves the words of physicians whose own books are lost.
explanation:
Oribasius studied medicine in Alexandria under Zeno of Cyprus and became personal physician to Julian, serving him from 361 until the emperor's death in 363. Julian, who hoped to revive the classical past, commissioned him to gather the best of Greek medical writing. The result was the Medical Collections (Iatrikai Synagogai, or Collectiones medicae), which excerpted and arranged the earlier literature. After Julian's death Oribasius fell from favour for a time and was later recalled by the emperor Valens.

Oribasius was a compiler rather than an original writer, and that is what makes the work valuable: it preserves selections from physicians such as Antyllus, Archigenes, Diocles and Rufus of Ephesus, whose own books no longer exist. He also wrote shorter digests, including a nine-book Synopsis for Eustathius, which carried this material into Byzantine medicine.

date.basis: Commissioned by Julian, whom Oribasius served from 361 to 363; when the compilation was finished is not recorded.

locationNote: Mapped to Pergamon, the city the sources associate him with; where he compiled the work is not recorded in the sources consulted.

people.name: Julian
people.role: Roman emperor who commissioned the work

whatChanged: The scattered Greek medical literature was gathered into one large reference compiled from many authors.
whyItMattered: Much of what is known about several lost Greek physicians survives only through Oribasius's excerpts, and his digests carried Greek medicine into the Byzantine world.
limitations: Oribasius compiled other writers' work and added little of his own.
Only part of the 70 books survives.

sources.supports: Surviving books of the Collectiones; selections from physicians whose works no longer exist, including Antyllus, Archigenes and Diocles; studied at Alexandria under Zeno; physician to Julian; recalled by Valens; the encyclopedia a product of the effort of Julian and his circle to recall the classical past.

title: Basil of Caesarea builds the Basileias
summary: After the famine of 369, Basil of Caesarea built a charitable complex outside the city, with houses for the poor, the sick and travellers and a section for people with leprosy. Physicians and nurses treated the sick there, and many historians regard it as one of the first hospitals.
explanation:
In 369 a severe famine struck Cappadocia, and Basil, then a priest, gathered the poor and fed them. After becoming bishop of Caesarea in 370 he built a complex just outside the city, which his friend Gregory of Nazianzus called a 'new city'. It held a church, houses for the poor, the sick and travellers, workshops, and a part set aside for people with leprosy, whom Basil cared for himself. Physicians and nurses treated the sick there.

A letter of 372 shows the building well under way, and Gregory's funeral oration for Basil in 379 is the fullest description of it. Some years earlier the emperor Julian had written to a pagan high priest urging pagans to match the Christians' care for strangers, a sign that Christian charitable houses were already spreading in the Greek East.

date.basis: Begun after the famine of 369; a letter of 372 shows construction well under way.

whatChanged: Care for the sick, the poor and people with leprosy was gathered into a permanent institution with medical staff.
whyItMattered: It is the best-documented early example of the Christian hospital, an institution that went on to spread through the Byzantine world and beyond.
limitations: Whether it was the first hospital depends on the definition used; Basil himself called it a shelter for the poor (ptochotropheion).
The evidence comes from a few letters and Gregory's praise of his friend, not from records of the institution.

title: Ephrem sets up a famine hospital in Edessa
summary: When famine struck Edessa in the winter of 372–373, the deacon and hymn writer Ephrem the Syrian shamed the city's rich into giving, then set up about 300 beds in the public porticoes, where he nursed the starving and the sick. He died soon afterwards, probably in June 373.
explanation:
Ephrem moved from Nisibis to Edessa, in northern Mesopotamia, in 363 and lived as a hermit near the city while serving its church as a deacon; he is remembered above all for his hymns. When famine struck Edessa in the winter of 372–373 he left his cell, rebuked the rich for letting the poor die while they hoarded grain, and used the money they gave him to set up about 300 beds in the public porticoes. There he nursed the starving and the sick himself.

The church historian Sozomen tells the story in the fifth century. It shows that within a few years of Basil's foundation at Caesarea, Christian leaders in Syria were also organising care for the sick in buildings set aside for it.

date.basis: The famine of winter 372–373; Ephrem died soon afterwards, probably in June 373.

whatChanged: An emergency hospital was organised in a city's public buildings to care for famine victims.
whyItMattered: It is an early example of a temporary hospital set up in a crisis, and of hospital care spreading through the Christian East.
limitations: The account comes from church histories and lives of the saint, not from records of the relief, and details such as the number of beds may be rounded or idealised.
The Chronicle of Edessa dates his death to June 373, but 378 and 379 are also given.

sources.supports: When Edessa was severely visited by famine, Ephrem left his solitary cell and rebuked the rich for letting the poor die instead of sharing their surplus.

title: Fabiola founds a hospital in Rome
summary: In the 390s the Roman noblewoman Fabiola used her wealth to found a hospital in Rome, where she gathered the sick from the streets and nursed them herself. With Pammachius she also founded a hospice for travellers at Portus, Rome's harbour. Jerome's letter about her is the main source.
explanation:
Fabiola came from a leading Roman family and, after the death of her second husband, devoted her fortune to charity. In Rome she opened a nosocomeion, a house for the sick, apparently the first in the city. According to Jerome she gathered the sick from the streets and waited on them herself, not shunning even repulsive wounds and sores. With her friend Pammachius she also set up a hospice for strangers (xenodochium) at Portus, the harbour of Rome.

Jerome described her work in a eulogy written to her relative Oceanus (Letter 77) after her death in 399. It shows the hospital, which had appeared first in the Christian East, reaching the Latin West within a generation of Basil's foundation at Caesarea.

Almost everything known comes from Jerome's letters.
